triage.name: Bipolar Disorder
triage.reason: Major psychiatric illness with manic or depressive episodes; diagnosis by careful history of mood episodes, sleep and function, with strong safety and differential teaching.

review_issues: auto-repaired: labs: dropped 'ua_tox' (not in the reference table)

demographics: Affects men and women at roughly equal rates
Onset is typically in late adolescence or early adulthood
Bipolar I disorder tends to present at a slightly younger age and with more manic episodes in men
Bipolar II disorder with prominent depression and hypomania is diagnosed more often in women
More than one in four first episodes occur after age 50

risk_factors.text: Major depressive episodes, especially early onset or postpartum
Childhood trauma or major stressful life events
Substance use, particularly stimulants or cannabis
Antidepressant treatment that triggers mania or hypomania
Disrupted circadian rhythm or sleep deprivation

family_history: Bipolar disorder in a first-degree relative
Major depressive disorder in a first-degree relative
Psychotic disorders in a first-degree relative
social_history: Recent major life stressor or loss
Irregular sleep schedule or shift work

chief_complaints.text: I go from feeling on top of the world to not being able to get out of bed
My family says I've been acting completely different
I haven't slept in days and I feel like I don't need to
I feel worthless and can't do anything
My thoughts are racing and I can't slow down
I spent money I don't have and can't explain why

hpi.onset: Episodic mood changes beginning in late adolescence or early adulthood; a first episode may be manic, hypomanic, mixed, or depressive
hpi.duration: Manic episodes last at least a week (or require hospitalization); hypomanic episodes last at least 4 days; depressive episodes typically last at least 2 weeks; episodes recur over a lifetime
hpi.progression: Discrete episodes of elevated, irritable, or depressed mood separated by periods of normal mood; episode frequency and severity vary, and some patients cycle rapidly with four or more episodes per year
hpi.quality: Distinct periods of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy, alternating with periods of low mood, anhedonia, and low energy
hpi.severity: Ranges from mild hypomania that others notice but the patient may not, to severe mania with psychosis or dangerous behavior, and to major depression with suicidal thinking
hpi.timing: Symptoms occur most of the day, nearly every day, during an episode; mood and energy are often worse in the morning during depression and sleep need is markedly reduced during mania

associated_symptoms.text: Impulsive or risky behavior such as spending, sex, or driving
Loss of interest or pleasure in usual activities
Psychotic symptoms such as delusions or hallucinations

pertinent_negatives: Symptoms only during substance use or withdrawal
Mood elevation only while taking an antidepressant
Continuous depressed mood for more than two years without elevated episodes
No discrete episodes, with mood symptoms that are chronic and stable
Medical cause of mood change such as thyroid disease or steroid use
Delusions or hallucinations lasting more than two weeks without mood symptoms

atypical.how_it_differs: Children may present with irritability, rapid mood shifts, and behavioral problems rather than clear episodes; mania can look like severe ADHD or oppositional behavior.
missing_classic_features: Grandiosity described as unusual for age

atypical.how_it_differs: First episodes after age 50 are less common and more often present with depression or confusion; mania may be mistaken for dementia or delirium, and medical causes and medications must be excluded.
Mood episodes may occur during pregnancy or postpartum; postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency, and medication decisions must weigh fetal and breastfeeding risks.

general.mild: Well-groomed, talkative, mildly elevated mood or mild psychomotor slowing; no distress
general.moderate: Pressured speech, restless or slowed movement, irritable or tearful, disheveled at times
general.severe: Markedly elevated or depressed, poor attention, disorganized or agitated, may require redirection
general.critical: Acutely agitated or catatonic, unable to cooperate with exam, risk of harm to self or others

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to describe their mood over the past week
findings.finding: Reports feeling unusually high, elated, expansive, or extremely irritable

findings.maneuver: Observe the rate, volume, and pressure of speech during the interview
Ask an open-ended question and follow the patient's train of thought
findings.finding: Thoughts jump rapidly from one topic to another with only loose connections

findings.maneuver: Ask about self-perception, abilities, and plans
findings.finding: Inflated self-esteem or grandiose beliefs out of proportion to reality

findings.maneuver: Ask how many hours the patient sleeps and whether they feel rested
findings.finding: Sleeps only a few hours but reports feeling rested and energetic

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient's activity level and ability to sit still
findings.finding: Restless, pacing, unable to remain seated

findings.maneuver: Ask about sadness, hopelessness, and loss of interest
Observe movement and speech speed during the interview
findings.finding: Slowed movement, long pauses before answering, soft monotonous speech

findings.maneuver: Ask directly about thoughts of death, self-harm, or suicide
findings.finding: Expresses suicidal thoughts or a plan

findings.maneuver: Ask about hearing voices or unusual beliefs; assess reality testing
Observe for immobility, mutism, posturing, or negativism
findings.finding: Decreased responsiveness, posturing, or waxy flexibility

findings.finding: No focal deficits, tremor, or abnormal reflexes

findings.maneuver: Palpate the thyroid and inspect for goiter or eye signs
findings.finding: No goiter, lid lag, or proptosis
Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, clear lungs

labs.caveat: Low TSH with elevated free T4 suggests hyperthyroidism, which can mimic mania; a normal TSH makes thyroid disease unlikely.
Elevated free T4 with suppressed TSH supports hyperthyroidism rather than bipolar disorder.
Positive in pregnancy; pregnancy and postpartum period affect mood and medication choices. Not a cause of mania but must be known before treatment.
Hyperglycemia may reflect metabolic syndrome or diabetes, common comorbidities and relevant to medication selection.
Elevated A1c supports diabetes or prediabetes, which affects choice of mood stabilizer.
Elevated creatinine indicates renal impairment, which affects dosing of lithium and other medications.
Hypercalcemia can cause mood changes, confusion, and lethargy that mimic psychiatric illness.
Elevated morning cortisol suggests Cushing syndrome, which can present with depression, mania, or psychosis.
Low B12 can cause mood and cognitive symptoms; replace if deficient.
Low folate is associated with depressive symptoms and poor response to treatment.

findings.text: No acute infarct, hemorrhage, or mass

initial.why: Screens for thyroid disease, a common reversible cause of mood symptoms
Baseline electrolytes and renal function before starting mood stabilizers
Baseline blood counts; some psychotropic medications can affect them
Detects stimulant or other substance use that can cause or mimic mania

initial.only_if: patient is a woman of childbearing age

supporting.why: Confirms hyperthyroidism if TSH is abnormal
Renal function before lithium or other renally cleared drugs
Screens for hypercalcemia, which can cause psychiatric symptoms
Screens for diabetes, a common comorbidity affecting medication choice
Deficiency can contribute to mood and cognitive symptoms
Deficiency can contribute to depressive symptoms
Screens for Cushing syndrome if clinical features suggest it
supporting.only_if: features of Cushing syndrome are present

not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for focal neurologic findings or atypical presentation
not_indicated.only_if: focal neurologic deficits or atypical features are present

not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for acute neurologic change or head trauma
not_indicated.only_if: acute neurologic change or head trauma is present

not_indicated.why: Not indicated unless CNS infection or inflammation is suspected
Not indicated unless seizures are suspected

decision_points: Always assess suicide risk and safety
Rule out substance-induced mood disorder with urine toxicology
Check TSH and free T4 to exclude thyroid disease
Check pregnancy status before prescribing mood stabilizers in women of childbearing age
Consider MRI or CT brain only if focal neurologic signs or atypical presentation

criteria.name: Manic episode
criteria.summary: A distinct period of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy lasting at least one week (or any duration if hospitalization is needed), with at least three of: grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity, or risky behavior; causes marked impairment or requires hospitalization.

criteria.name: Hypomanic episode
criteria.summary: A distinct period of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy lasting at least four days, with similar but less severe symptoms; not severe enough to cause marked impairment or require hospitalization, but noticeable to others.

criteria.name: Major depressive episode
criteria.summary: At least two weeks of depressed mood or loss of interest, with at least four of: appetite or weight change, sleep disturbance, psychomotor changes, fatigue, worthlessness or guilt, poor concentration, or suicidal thoughts.

criteria.name: Bipolar I disorder
criteria.summary: At least one manic episode; depressive or hypomanic episodes may also occur.

criteria.name: Bipolar II disorder
criteria.summary: At least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode; no full manic episode.

criteria.name: Cyclothymic disorder
criteria.summary: At least two years (one year in youth) of numerous periods with hypomanic symptoms and depressive symptoms that do not meet full criteria for a manic, hypomanic, or major depressive episode.

differential.name: Major depressive disorder
differential.why_considered: Depressive episodes are common in bipolar disorder and often bring the patient to care first; recurrent depression can look identical until an elevated episode is uncovered.
differential.trigger: Any patient presenting with depression, especially early onset, atypical, or treatment-resistant depression

history: No lifetime manic or hypomanic episode
No discrete periods of decreased need for sleep with increased energy
Depression is the only mood polarity
Family history of depression rather than bipolar disorder
exam: Depressed mood or anhedonia without elevated, expansive, or irritable mood
Psychomotor retardation or agitation without pressured speech or flight of ideas
labs: No substance or medication trigger for mood elevation

differential.name: Substance-induced mood disorder
differential.why_considered: Stimulants, cannabis, alcohol, and withdrawal states can produce elevated, irritable, or depressed mood that mimics a mood episode.
differential.trigger: Mood symptoms that begin during or shortly after substance use or withdrawal

history: Temporal link between substance use or withdrawal and mood symptoms
Symptoms resolve with sustained abstinence
No prior discrete mood episodes independent of substance use
exam: Mood changes track with substance use rather than a spontaneous episode
labs: Positive urine toxicology for stimulants, cannabis, or other substances

differential.name: Schizophrenia
differential.why_considered: Psychotic symptoms occur in severe mania and can be mistaken for a primary psychotic disorder.
differential.trigger: Psychosis with prominent mood symptoms or a history of mood episodes

history: Psychosis occurs only during mood episodes in bipolar disorder
Prominent and persistent mood symptoms
Delusions or hallucinations lasting more than two weeks without mood symptoms suggests schizophrenia
exam: Mood-congruent grandiosity or elevated mood during psychosis
Negative symptoms such as flat affect are more prominent in schizophrenia

differential.name: Schizoaffective disorder
differential.why_considered: Combines psychotic and mood symptoms, overlapping heavily with bipolar disorder with psychotic features.

history: Delusions or hallucinations for at least two weeks in the absence of mood symptoms
Mood episodes present for the majority of the illness duration
Psychosis persists beyond mood episodes
exam: Psychotic symptoms may be present even when mood is euthymic

differential.name: Hyperthyroidism
differential.why_considered: Thyroid disease can cause irritability, insomnia, weight loss, palpitations, and mood elevation that mimic mania.

history: Heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations, weight loss despite increased appetite
No discrete mood episodes with periods of normal mood
exam: Goiter, lid lag, proptosis, fine tremor, tachycardia
labs: Low TSH with elevated free T4

differential.name: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
differential.why_considered: Chronic hyperactivity, impulsivity, and distractibility can be confused with hypomania, especially in children and young adults.

history: Symptoms are chronic and lifelong rather than episodic
No discrete periods of elevated mood with decreased need for sleep
Symptoms present before age 12
exam: Hyperactivity and inattention without mood elevation or grandiosity

differential.name: Borderline personality disorder
differential.why_considered: Mood instability, impulsivity, and irritability can resemble rapid mood shifts.

history: Mood shifts are rapid and reactive to interpersonal triggers rather than sustained episodes
Chronic feelings of emptiness, fear of abandonment, identity disturbance
No discrete episodes lasting days to weeks
exam: Mood changes within minutes to hours rather than days

differential.name: Cushing syndrome
differential.why_considered: Excess cortisol can cause depression, mania, or psychosis along with insomnia and irritability.

history: Weight gain, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness, striae
Recent corticosteroid use
exam: Central obesity, moon facies, buffalo hump, purple striae, hypertension
labs: Elevated morning cortisol or failed dexamethasone suppression

differential.name: Delirium
differential.why_considered: Acute confusion, agitation, and mood lability can be mistaken for mania, especially in older adults.
differential.trigger: Acute onset of confusion or agitation with fluctuating attention

history: Acute onset over hours to days
Fluctuating course with inattention
Recent infection, medication change, or metabolic disturbance
exam: Disorientation, fluctuating attention, altered level of consciousness
labs: Abnormal CBC, BMP, or urinalysis suggesting infection or metabolic cause

severity.mild: Hypomanic or mild depressive symptoms that are noticeable to others but do not cause marked impairment; the patient can function at work and home with support.
severity.moderate: Clear manic or major depressive episode with significant impairment in work, relationships, or self-care; no psychosis and no immediate danger.
severity.severe: Mania with psychosis, dangerous impulsivity, or severe depression with inability to care for self; requires hospitalization or intensive treatment.
severity.critical: Life-threatening: catatonia, severe self-harm or suicide attempt, dangerous agitation, or medical complications such as dehydration or neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

red_flags.finding: Suicidal ideation with plan or intent
red_flags.meaning: Immediate risk of self-harm; requires emergency psychiatric evaluation and safety planning

red_flags.finding: Psychosis with command hallucinations or dangerous grandiosity
red_flags.meaning: Risk of harm to self or others; needs urgent hospitalization
Medical emergency; can lead to dehydration, rhabdomyolysis, and death without treatment
Risk of injury; requires acute stabilization

red_flags.finding: Inability to maintain nutrition or hydration
red_flags.meaning: Medical compromise during a prolonged episode; may need inpatient care

red_flags.finding: Rapid cycling with four or more episodes per year
red_flags.meaning: More difficult to treat and associated with higher morbidity

complications.name: Substance use disorder
clues: Alcohol or drug use during mood episodes

complications.name: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
clues: Elevated creatine kinase after antipsychotic use

complications.name: Cognitive impairment
clues: Complaints of memory and concentration problems between episodes

special_populations.differences: May present with irritability, rapid mood shifts, and behavioral problems rather than clear episodes; mania can resemble severe ADHD or oppositional behavior, and diagnosis requires careful longitudinal history.
First episodes after age 50 are less common and more often present with depression or confusion; mania may be mistaken for dementia or delirium, and medical causes and medications must be excluded.
Mood episodes may occur during pregnancy or postpartum; postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency, and medication decisions must weigh fetal and breastfeeding risks.

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a period of at least several days when you felt unusually high, elated, or extremely irritable, and had much more energy than usual?
key_questions.looking_for: A discrete episode of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy and activity, distinct from the patient's baseline

key_questions.question: How long did that period last, and did it last most of the day nearly every day?
key_questions.looking_for: At least one week for mania (or any duration if hospitalization was needed); at least four days for hypomania

key_questions.question: During that time, how much sleep did you need, and did you still feel rested?
key_questions.looking_for: A decreased need for sleep, sleeping only a few hours yet feeling energized, which strongly supports a manic or hypomanic episode

key_questions.question: Did you talk more or faster than usual, or feel like your thoughts were racing?
key_questions.looking_for: Pressured speech, rapid speech, or flight of ideas during the elevated period

key_questions.question: Did you feel unusually confident, powerful, or capable of things others thought were unrealistic?
key_questions.looking_for: Grandiosity or inflated self-esteem out of proportion to reality

key_questions.question: Did you do anything risky or out of character, like spending large amounts of money, reckless driving, or sexual behavior you later regretted?
key_questions.looking_for: Impulsive, risky, or poor-judgment behavior during the elevated period

key_questions.question: Have you also had periods of at least two weeks when you felt very sad, hopeless, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy?
key_questions.looking_for: A major depressive episode, which is common in bipolar disorder and often brings the patient to care first

key_questions.question: Did other people notice or comment that you were acting differently during these periods?
key_questions.looking_for: Observable change noticed by family or friends, which supports that the episode was a distinct change from baseline

key_questions.question: Were you ever hospitalized or treated urgently because of your mood or behavior?
key_questions.looking_for: Hospitalization for mania supports bipolar I disorder; no hospitalization with shorter episodes suggests hypomania

key_questions.question: Have you ever heard voices or had unusual beliefs that others did not share, and did that happen only during mood episodes?
key_questions.looking_for: Psychosis occurring only during mood episodes supports bipolar disorder; psychosis lasting more than two weeks without mood symptoms suggests schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder

key_questions.question: Have you had thoughts of death, self-harm, or suicide?
key_questions.looking_for: Suicidal ideation, plan, or intent, which requires immediate safety assessment and emergency evaluation

key_questions.question: Have you ever been diagnosed with depression, anxiety, or ADHD, and what were you told about it?
key_questions.looking_for: A prior diagnosis of depression or ADHD that may actually reflect unrecognized bipolar disorder

key_questions.question: Have you ever taken an antidepressant, and did it seem to trigger unusual energy, irritability, or not sleeping?
key_questions.looking_for: Antidepressant-associated mania or hypomania, which supports a bipolar diathesis

key_questions.question: Have you ever taken steroids, thyroid medicine, or stimulants?
key_questions.looking_for: Medications that can cause or mimic mood elevation, such as corticosteroids, levothyroxine, or stimulants

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have bipolar disorder, depression, psychosis, or die by suicide?
key_questions.looking_for: A first-degree relative with bipolar disorder or related psychiatric illness, which raises risk

key_questions.question: How much alcohol or drugs do you use, and do your mood symptoms happen only when you are using or withdrawing?
key_questions.looking_for: Substance use that could cause or mimic mood episodes; symptoms that occur only with use or withdrawal suggest substance-induced mood disorder

key_questions.question: Have you recently had a major stressor, loss, or a change in your sleep schedule, such as shift work?
key_questions.looking_for: Stressors or circadian disruption that may precipitate episodes

key_questions.question: If you could be pregnant, when was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy status, which affects medication selection and safety

reasoning_points: A discrete episode of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy and activity lasting at least one week (or any duration if hospitalization was needed) for mania, or at least four days for hypomania

At least three additional symptoms during the elevated period, such as grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity, or risky behavior
A decreased need for sleep with continued feeling of being rested, which is a hallmark of mania and hypomania
The presence of at least one major depressive episode, which is common and often the reason the patient seeks care
Symptoms cause marked impairment or require hospitalization in mania, but not in hypomania
Psychosis, if present, occurs only during mood episodes rather than independently
Substance use and medications such as corticosteroids, levothyroxine, or stimulants have been considered and excluded as the cause
Thyroid disease and other medical causes of mood change have been excluded with history and laboratory testing
Suicide risk and safety have been assessed directly
The pattern of discrete episodes separated by periods of normal mood distinguishes bipolar disorder from chronic mood instability or personality-related mood shifts

easy: Young adult with a clear history of a week-long episode of elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, and risky spending
Clear alternation between elevated and depressed episodes with normal mood in between
medium: Patient presents with depression and only on careful questioning reveals a past hypomanic episode
Bipolar II disorder with prominent depression and subtle hypomania
Substance use that complicates the timeline of mood episodes
hard: Older adult with a first episode of mania or confusion, requiring exclusion of delirium, dementia, and medical causes
Psychosis that raises the question of schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder
Rapid cycling with four or more episodes per year
Mixed episode with simultaneous depressive and manic symptoms
Postpartum presentation with mood elevation or psychosis
